A Terry stop or a roadside traffic stop is generally not custody (Berkemer). Volunteered statements are always admissible. Read the card, don't paraphrase, record it, and record the waiver.

cases.name: Berkemer v. McCarty
cases.facts: An Ohio State Highway Patrol trooper stopped Richard McCarty near Columbus for weaving, had him do field sobriety tests, and asked if he'd been using intoxicants; McCarty said he'd had two beers and smoked marijuana. He was arrested, taken to the jail, and questioned more without Miranda warnings.
cases.held: Miranda applies to custodial interrogation for misdemeanor traffic offenses the same as felonies. But a routine roadside traffic stop is not 'custody' for Miranda, because it is brief, public, and typically involves one or two officers; roadside questioning before arrest doesn't require warnings. Once the driver is arrested, questioning requires Miranda.
cases.forUs: Roadside questions during a normal stop ('how much have you had tonight?') don't need Miranda. Once you cuff them or tell them they're under arrest, they do. The gray zone is when a stop becomes custody-like: multiple officers, guns, cuffs, long duration, moving them to the car. If you've escalated to that, Mirandize before asking more.
notes: Ohio case: the stop was on I-270 in Franklin County.

cases.name: Rhode Island v. Innis
cases.facts: Thomas Innis was arrested for a shotgun murder, Mirandized, and invoked. In the car, two officers talked to each other about how terrible it would be if a child from the nearby school for disabled kids found the missing shotgun. Innis told them to turn around and showed them the gun.
cases.held: 'Interrogation' under Miranda means express questioning or any words or actions the officer should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response. Here, the brief conversation between officers did not rise to that level.
cases.forUs: Interrogation is about what your words are likely to produce, not whether you phrased them as a question. Talking 'to your partner' in front of a suspect about the case is risky; so are 'appeals to conscience.' After invocation, the safe conversation is logistics only. Routine booking questions (name, DOB, address) are not interrogation.

cases.name: Edwards v. Arizona / Davis v. United States / Maryland v. Shatzer
cases.facts: Edwards: a suspect asked for a lawyer; the next morning detectives came back, re-Mirandized him, and got a confession. Davis: during an NCIS interview the suspect said 'Maybe I should talk to a lawyer,' and agents continued after clarifying. Shatzer: a prisoner invoked counsel; two and a half years later a different detective re-approached him in prison and he confessed.
cases.held: Once a suspect clearly invokes the right to counsel, police must stop and may not re-initiate interrogation unless the suspect does, or counsel is present (Edwards). The invocation must be unambiguous; an equivocal reference to a lawyer doesn't require stopping, though clarifying is good practice (Davis). The Edwards protection ends after a 14-day break in custody (Shatzer).
cases.forUs: 'I want a lawyer' means stop, period, and don't come back later to try again unless they reach out to you. 'Maybe I should get a lawyer' is ambiguous; you can keep going, but asking 'are you asking for a lawyer?' protects the statement. Flag invocations in the report so the next detective knows. Fourteen days out of custody resets the clock.

cases.name: Berghuis v. Thompkins / Salinas v. Texas
cases.facts: Thompkins: a murder suspect was Mirandized, declined to sign a waiver, and stayed nearly silent for almost three hours before answering 'yes' when asked if he prayed to God for forgiveness for the shooting. Salinas: in a voluntary, non-custodial interview, a suspect answered questions but went silent when asked if ballistics would match his shotgun; the prosecutor used the silence at trial.
cases.held: Silence alone is not an invocation of the right to remain silent; the suspect must unambiguously invoke it. A suspect who understands his rights and then answers questions has impliedly waived (Thompkins). In a non-custodial setting, a suspect who simply stops answering, without expressly invoking the privilege, can have that silence used against him (Salinas).
cases.forUs: Sitting silent after warnings isn't an invocation; if they later talk, it's a waiver. But document that they understood the warnings. In a voluntary interview, note exactly which questions they answered and where they stopped. If they say anything like 'I'm not answering that' or 'I'm done talking,' treat it as an invocation.

cases.name: Missouri v. Seibert / Oregon v. Elstad
cases.facts: Elstad: officers arrested a teen at home for burglary; one remarked he thought the teen was involved, and the teen said 'Yes, I was there.' At the station he was Mirandized and gave a full written confession. Seibert: a Missouri department trained officers to deliberately question first, get a confession, then Mirandize and have the suspect repeat it.
cases.held: A voluntary unwarned statement does not automatically taint a later, properly warned statement (Elstad). But a deliberate 'question first, warn later' technique designed to undermine Miranda renders the post-warning statement inadmissible (Seibert).
cases.forUs: If someone blurts something out before you've warned them, you can still Mirandize and take a proper statement afterward. What you can't do is question first on purpose and then 'clean it up' with warnings. In Ohio, remember Farris: the physical evidence from an unwarned custodial statement is also out, unlike the federal rule.

cases.name: State v. Farris
cases.facts: A trooper stopped Blake Farris for speeding, smelled burnt marijuana, took his keys, patted him down, put him in the cruiser, and, without Miranda, asked about the marijuana. Farris admitted there was a pipe in the trunk. The trooper Mirandized him, asked again, got the same answer, and searched the trunk.
cases.held: Farris was in custody once the trooper took his keys, patted him down, placed him in the cruiser, and told him he'd be searching the car. Under Article I, Section 10 of the Ohio Constitution, physical evidence found as a direct result of an unwarned custodial statement is inadmissible, rejecting the federal rule from United States v. Patane. The second, warned statement was also tainted because it was the same question asked immediately after the first.
cases.forUs: Ohio goes further than the Supreme Court: if you get an unwarned custodial admission and it leads you to the gun or the drugs, Ohio suppresses the gun or the drugs too. Also note what made Farris 'custody' on a traffic stop: keys taken, frisk, placed in cruiser, told the car would be searched. If you've done those things, Mirandize before asking where the contraband is.
notes: In re T.D.S. (2024-Ohio-4799) reaffirmed Farris in a juvenile case.

cases.name: New York v. Quarles
cases.facts: A rape victim told officers her attacker had a gun and had run into a supermarket. Officers found Benjamin Quarles inside, frisked him, found an empty holster, cuffed him, and asked 'Where's the gun?' before any warnings. He nodded toward some cartons.
cases.held: There is a public-safety exception to Miranda: when officers ask questions reasonably prompted by a concern for public safety (a loose gun in a public place), the answers and the evidence are admissible even though the suspect was in custody and unwarned.
cases.forUs: 'Where's the gun?' right after a weapon-related arrest, before warnings, is fine when there's a real safety reason: a gun somewhere a kid or an accomplice could get it. Keep it to the safety question; once you start asking about the crime, you've left the exception. Articulate the danger in the report.

cases.name: J.D.B. v. North Carolina
cases.facts: A 13-year-old special-education student was pulled from class by a uniformed school resource officer and questioned for at least 30 minutes in a closed conference room by an investigator and school officials about burglaries, without Miranda warnings or a parent. He confessed.
cases.held: A child's age, when known to the officer or objectively apparent, must be considered in the Miranda custody analysis. A reasonable child may feel unable to leave in circumstances where an adult would not.
cases.forUs: The 'would a reasonable person feel free to leave' question is 'would a reasonable kid this age.' Schools, closed rooms, uniforms, and no parent push toward custody. Follow 405.1 on parental notification and juvenile interviews; Ohio courts look closely at juvenile waivers (In re T.D.S. applied Farris to a juvenile).

cases.name: Vega v. Tekoh
cases.facts: A deputy questioned a hospital worker about a sexual-assault allegation without Miranda warnings and got a written statement. The statement was used at trial; the worker was acquitted and then sued the deputy under § 1983 for the Miranda violation.
cases.held: A Miranda violation is not itself a basis for a § 1983 civil suit; Miranda is a prophylactic rule whose remedy is suppression at trial, not damages.
cases.forUs: Skipping Miranda won't by itself get you sued in federal court, but it will lose the statement (and in Ohio, under Farris, the evidence it led to), and coerced statements are still a due-process violation that can be sued on. Don't read this as permission to skip warnings.

cases.name: Illinois v. Perkins / Howes v. Fields / Montejo v. Louisiana
cases.facts: Perkins: an undercover officer placed in a cellblock got a murder suspect to brag about a killing. Fields: a Michigan inmate was taken to a conference room and questioned by sheriff's deputies for five to seven hours about an unrelated crime, told he could return to his cell anytime. Montejo: a defendant who had counsel appointed at arraignment was later Mirandized by detectives and agreed to go with them to find the murder weapon.
cases.held: Miranda doesn't apply when a suspect doesn't know he's talking to police; no coercion exists (Perkins). Being in prison does not automatically mean 'custody' for Miranda; it depends on the circumstances of the questioning (Fields). A defendant who has been appointed counsel can still be approached and waive Miranda for police questioning; the old rule barring it (Michigan v. Jackson) is overruled (Montejo).
cases.forUs: Jail interviews still need the custody analysis; tell the inmate he can end it and return to his cell, and document it. Someone with a lawyer on the case can still waive and talk to you if he hasn't invoked under Edwards, but coordinate with the prosecutor first because Sixth Amendment issues attach once charges are filed. Don't use informants to deliberately elicit statements from a charged defendant (Massiah).

cases.name: Mapp v. Ohio
cases.facts: Cleveland officers went to Dollree Mapp's house looking for a bombing suspect and gambling materials. She refused entry without a warrant. Three hours later, more officers forced the door, waved a piece of paper they claimed was a warrant (it never surfaced), handcuffed her when she grabbed it, and searched the whole house. They found 'obscene' books in a trunk and charged her with possession.
cases.held: The exclusionary rule applies to the states: evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible in state criminal prosecutions.
cases.forUs: Cleveland, 1957. This is why the suppression hearing exists. Every search-and-seizure case in this section matters because of Mapp: get it wrong and the evidence disappears, and under Wong Sun so does whatever flowed from it.

cases.name: Wong Sun v. United States / Nix v. Williams / Murray v. United States
cases.facts: Wong Sun: agents made an illegal entry and arrest, got statements leading to another suspect and to heroin. Nix: after an improper interrogation (the 'Christian burial speech'), the defendant led officers to a child's body; 200 searchers were already combing the area in a grid that would have reached it. Murray: agents entered a warehouse illegally, saw marijuana, left, and then got a warrant based only on information they had before the illegal entry.
cases.held: Evidence derived from an illegal search or seizure is 'fruit of the poisonous tree' and is suppressed unless the connection is sufficiently attenuated (Wong Sun). Illegally obtained evidence is admissible if the state proves it would inevitably have been discovered by lawful means (Nix). Evidence is admissible if it was also obtained from a genuinely independent lawful source (Murray).
cases.forUs: A bad stop or entry poisons what follows, including statements and later finds. The rescue doctrines (inevitable discovery, independent source, attenuation) are real but require proof: a tow that was already going to happen, a warrant already in process, an intervening event. If you realize you've made an error, stop, don't compound it, and talk to a supervisor about a lawful path before going further.

cases.name: Herring v. United States / Davis v. United States / United States v. Leon
cases.facts: Leon: officers executed a facially valid search warrant that was later held to lack probable cause. Herring: an officer arrested a man on a warrant that a neighboring county's database showed active but had actually been recalled months earlier; the search incident found meth and a gun. Davis: officers did a vehicle search that was lawful under then-binding precedent, which the Supreme Court later changed in Gant.
cases.held: The exclusionary rule doesn't apply when officers reasonably rely on a warrant later found defective (Leon), on a database error that is isolated negligence rather than systemic or reckless (Herring), or on binding appellate precedent later overruled (Davis). Exclusion is meant to deter deliberate, reckless, or grossly negligent police conduct.
cases.forUs: Good-faith reliance on a warrant, a records system, or existing law protects the evidence when the mistake wasn't yours. It does not protect sloppy affidavits, 'I thought the warrant was still good' when you could have checked, or recurring records problems. Confirm warrants through dispatch before acting on them and note the confirmation time. Ohio courts generally follow the good-faith exception but apply it to Ohio-specific rules too.

cases.name: Brady v. Maryland / Giglio v. United States
cases.facts: Brady: prosecutors withheld a co-defendant's confession that he, not Brady, did the actual killing. Giglio: prosecutors failed to disclose a promise of leniency to the key witness.
cases.held: Due process requires the prosecution to disclose evidence favorable to the accused that is material to guilt or punishment (Brady), including evidence that impeaches the credibility of government witnesses (Giglio). The duty covers evidence known to police, not just the prosecutor.
cases.forUs: Anything that helps the defense or hurts a witness's credibility has to get to the prosecutor, including your own sustained findings for dishonesty, inconsistent witness statements, and things that didn't make it into the report. 103.15 is the department's directive on this. A 'Brady/Giglio letter' can end a career because you can no longer testify; the fastest way to get one is a dishonesty finding.

cases.name: Neil v. Biggers / Manson v. Brathwaite / Perry v. New Hampshire
cases.facts: Biggers: a rape victim identified the defendant at a station-house show-up seven months after the attack. Brathwaite: an undercover officer identified a drug seller from a single photo left on his desk. Perry: a witness spontaneously identified a man standing next to a police officer in a parking lot; no police-arranged procedure.
cases.held: An unnecessarily suggestive identification procedure violates due process only if it creates a substantial likelihood of misidentification, judged by the witness's opportunity to view, degree of attention, accuracy of prior description, certainty, and time elapsed (Biggers/Brathwaite). Due-process screening applies only when police arranged the suggestive circumstances (Perry).
cases.forUs: One-on-one show-ups (402.3) are inherently suggestive and are tolerated because they're prompt. Keep them close in time, don't tell the witness you caught the guy, don't show the suspect in cuffs or in the back of a car if you can avoid it, bring the witness to the suspect, and get the witness's description before the show-up. Document certainty in the witness's own words. For photo arrays and lineups, Ohio statute controls (next entry).

cases.name: R.C. 2933.83 (Ohio lineup and photo-array statute)
cases.facts: Ohio's legislative response to wrongful-conviction research. It requires every law-enforcement agency that conducts live lineups or photo arrays to adopt written procedures.
cases.held: Required minimums: a blind or blinded administrator (someone who doesn't know who the suspect is, or a folder-shuffle method); the witness told that the suspect may or may not be present and that the investigation will continue regardless; fillers that match the description; a written record of the witness's own words about confidence and the result; and preservation of the array. Noncompliance is admissible to challenge the ID and the jury is instructed it may consider it, but it doesn't automatically suppress.
cases.forUs: Photo arrays are not something to throw together in the car. Use the department's procedure, a blind administrator or the folder method, the mandatory instruction, and record the witness's confidence statement verbatim. One-on-one show-ups aren't covered by the statute but 402.3 governs them. Failing the statute hands the defense a jury instruction that your ID is unreliable.

cases.name: Arizona v. Youngblood / California v. Trombetta
cases.facts: Youngblood: police failed to refrigerate a sexual-assault victim's clothing, and the semen samples degraded before they could be tested. Trombetta: officers did not preserve breath samples from Intoxilyzer tests.
cases.held: Failure to preserve potentially useful evidence violates due process only if the defendant shows bad faith on the part of police (Youngblood). There is no duty to preserve evidence whose exculpatory value was not apparent and for which comparable evidence remains available (Trombetta).
cases.forUs: Negligent loss of evidence usually won't dismiss the case, but it will hurt it, and bad faith (destroying something you knew could help the defense) will. Follow 407.1 on collection and storage, and if something is lost or degraded, document it immediately and honestly. BWC that 'wasn't activated' is treated with growing suspicion by Ohio courts and juries.

cases.name: Crawford v. Washington / Davis v. Washington / Hammon v. Indiana
cases.facts: Crawford: a wife's recorded statement to police describing a stabbing was played at trial when she didn't testify. Davis: a 911 caller described an ongoing assault by her ex-boyfriend as it happened; she didn't testify. Hammon: officers responded to a domestic call, found things calm, separated the couple, and had the wife describe what happened and sign an affidavit; she didn't testify.
cases.held: Testimonial out-of-court statements can't be used at trial unless the witness testifies or the defendant had a prior chance to cross-examine (Crawford). Statements made to resolve an ongoing emergency (the 911 call in Davis) are non-testimonial and admissible; statements describing past events once the scene is secure (Hammon) are testimonial and are not admissible without the witness.
cases.forUs: This is why DV cases die when the victim won't come to court. What you can save: the 911 recording, excited utterances made while the emergency is still live, injuries you photograph, the scene, the suspect's own statements, and what children or neighbors said in the moment. Once things are calm and you're doing the 'tell me what happened' interview, that statement needs her in court. Get the BWC rolling on arrival and capture the spontaneous stuff. Michigan v. Bryant (2011) extends 'ongoing emergency' to a shooting victim describing the shooter while he's still at large.

cases.name: Ohio v. Clark
cases.facts: A Cleveland preschool teacher noticed marks on a three-year-old and asked who did it; the child named 'Dee,' his mother's boyfriend. The teachers reported it. At trial the child was too young to testify, and the statements came in through the teachers.
cases.held: Statements by a very young child to a teacher about abuse, made primarily to address an ongoing concern for the child's safety and not to create evidence for prosecution, are non-testimonial and admissible even if the child doesn't testify. Mandatory-reporter status doesn't convert teachers into police agents.
cases.forUs: A child's spontaneous disclosure to a teacher, nurse, or parent about who hurt him is usable. Your own interview of a child is more likely to be testimonial; keep patrol questions to safety and immediate medical needs and leave the forensic interview to the trained team (401.35 and LCCS). Document who the child told first and exactly what was said.

cases.name: Giles v. California
cases.facts: Dwayne Giles shot and killed his ex-girlfriend. Weeks earlier she had told police he had assaulted and threatened to kill her. Prosecutors used those statements at the murder trial under 'forfeiture by wrongdoing.'
cases.held: A defendant forfeits his confrontation right only if he engaged in conduct designed to prevent the witness from testifying. Killing the witness isn't enough by itself unless the purpose was to keep her from testifying. But in DV cases, evidence of prior abuse and isolation intended to keep the victim from going to authorities can show that purpose.
cases.forUs: Documenting intimidation matters. If a DV suspect threatens the victim about calling police or going to court, write it down in the victim's words; that is what later lets her prior statements in if he silences her. Take 'if you call the cops I'll kill you' seriously as both a crime and future evidence.

cases.name: Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales / DeShaney v. Winnebago County
cases.facts: Castle Rock: Jessica Gonzales had a restraining order against her estranged husband. He took their three daughters. Over about eight hours she called and visited the police department repeatedly; officers told her to wait. He showed up at the station, opened fire, was killed, and the girls were found dead in his truck. DeShaney: social services returned a boy to a father they had repeatedly been warned was abusing him; he was beaten into permanent brain damage.
cases.held: There is generally no constitutional right to police protection from private violence (DeShaney). A protection order, even one with 'shall arrest' language, does not create a property interest enforceable under the Due Process Clause, so failure to enforce it is not a federal constitutional violation (Castle Rock).
cases.forUs: Federal civil liability for failing to act is limited, but that is not the standard you work to. Ohio law (R.C. 2935.03(B)(3)) makes DV and protection-order violations preferred-arrest offenses and requires you to document why you didn't arrest, and 401.5 is built on that. State tort claims and discipline are the real exposure. The lesson from Castle Rock is what not to do: eight hours of 'call back later.'

cases.name: Kallstrom v. City of Columbus (state-created danger)
cases.facts: Columbus released undercover officers' personnel files, including home addresses and family information, to defense counsel for a violent gang; the officers sued.
cases.held: The Sixth Circuit recognizes a 'state-created danger' exception to DeShaney: officials can be liable when their affirmative act creates or increases a special danger to a specific person, with deliberate indifference. The affirmative act must be directed at a specific victim, not the public at large.
cases.forUs: You generally can't be sued federally for not preventing harm, but you can be for creating it: leaving a drunk at the roadside in a dangerous spot after taking his keys, telling the abuser where the victim went, abandoning a passenger after arresting the driver in a bad area at night. Think about what your affirmative actions do to the people left behind on scene.

cases.name: In re Gault
cases.facts: Fifteen-year-old Gerald Gault was taken into custody for a lewd phone call while his parents were at work; they weren't notified. He was committed to a state school until 21 for an offense that carried a $50 fine for an adult, after hearings with no counsel, no sworn witnesses, and no record.
cases.held: Juveniles facing delinquency proceedings that may result in confinement are entitled to notice of charges, counsel, confrontation and cross-examination of witnesses, and the privilege against self-incrimination.
cases.forUs: Juveniles have the same core rights as adults plus extra protections. Ohio adds notification requirements (R.C. 2151.311) and 405.1 lays out parental contact, detention limits, and interview rules. Treat a juvenile interview as the most scrutinized statement you'll take.

cases.name: New Jersey v. T.L.O. / Safford Unified School District v. Redding
cases.facts: T.L.O.: a vice principal searched a 14-year-old's purse after she was caught smoking, found cigarettes, rolling papers, then marijuana and dealing notes. Redding: school officials strip-searched a 13-year-old girl to her underwear looking for prescription-strength ibuprofen based on another student's tip.
cases.held: School officials need only reasonable suspicion, not probable cause or a warrant, to search students, and the search must be reasonable in scope given the student's age and the nature of the infraction (T.L.O.). A strip search for non-dangerous pills on a thin tip is unreasonable (Redding).
cases.forUs: The relaxed school standard belongs to school officials. When a police officer (including an SRO) directs or conducts the search, courts increasingly apply the ordinary Fourth Amendment standards, and a search done 'at police request' can lose the T.L.O. protection. Don't use school staff as a workaround. Strip searches of juveniles follow 402.4 and need a very high bar.

cases.name: Juvenile interrogation: J.D.B. and In re T.D.S.
cases.facts: J.D.B.: a 13-year-old questioned at school without a parent or warnings (see Miranda section). T.D.S.: an Ohio juvenile made unwarned statements in custody that led police to physical evidence.
cases.held: Age is part of the custody analysis (J.D.B.). Ohio's Farris rule, excluding physical evidence derived from an unwarned custodial statement under the Ohio Constitution, applies fully to juveniles (T.D.S.).
cases.forUs: With kids, custody is found more readily and the fallout from skipping warnings is bigger in Ohio. Contact the parent per 405.1, warn before any custodial questioning, use plain language and confirm understanding, and record everything.

cases.name: Mental illness and the ADA: Sheehan and Sixth Circuit practice
cases.cite: City & County of San Francisco v. Sheehan, 575 U.S. 600 (2015)
cases.facts: Teresa Sheehan, in a group home, threatened a social worker with a knife during a psychiatric episode. Two officers entered her room, retreated when she came at them with the knife, then re-entered almost immediately rather than waiting for backup, pepper-sprayed her, and shot her when she kept coming.
cases.held: The officers were entitled to qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment claim: no clearly established law required them to wait or use different tactics when confronting an armed, dangerous person. The Court dismissed the ADA question without deciding whether the ADA requires accommodations during arrests.
cases.forUs: The Court didn't say the second entry was good tactics, only that it wasn't clearly unlawful. Time, distance, cover, and crisis-intervention skills are what 401.9 and your CIT training expect, and Champion v. Outlook Nashville (6th Cir.) says diminished capacity reduces the force a court will accept. Whether the ADA applies to on-scene arrests remains unsettled; act as if it does by making reasonable accommodations when safe.

cases.name: Emergency commitment: R.C. 5122.10 and State v. Dowell
cases.facts: R.C. 5122.10 lets an officer take a person into custody for emergency hospitalization when the officer has reason to believe the person is mentally ill and presents a substantial risk of harm to self or others. Dowell (see Arrests) involved a woman who physically resisted being taken in on a doctor's emergency form.
cases.held: The statute requires every reasonable and appropriate effort to take the person into custody in the least conspicuous manner, telling the person it's not a criminal arrest, who you are, and where they're going. Dowell holds that resisting that process can be charged as obstruction because the statute creates no privilege to impede officers.
cases.forUs: Narrate the required statements on BWC, use the least conspicuous means practicable, and get medical and CIT resources involved early. The authority to charge obstruction exists, but 401.9 and your discretion under 101.3 govern whether you should. A crisis call that ends in criminal charges will be reviewed hard.

cases.name: City of Houston v. Hill / Lewis v. City of New Orleans / Cohen v. California
cases.facts: Hill: a man shouted at officers to leave his friend alone and 'pick on somebody your own size'; he was arrested under an ordinance banning interrupting an officer. Lewis: a woman called an officer a 'G-D M-F police' and was charged under an ordinance against cursing at police. Cohen: a man wore a 'F--- the Draft' jacket in a courthouse.
cases.held: Speech critical of police, including profane and insulting speech, is protected; ordinances that criminalize interrupting or verbally challenging officers are unconstitutional. The First Amendment protects a significant amount of verbal criticism and challenge directed at police officers, and officers are expected to show more restraint than the average citizen (Hill). Only 'fighting words' likely to provoke immediate violence fall outside protection, and that category is very narrow when the target is a trained officer.
cases.forUs: Getting cussed at is part of the job and it is not disorderly conduct, obstruction, or anything else by itself. Ohio courts read R.C. 2917.11 the same way: words alone, directed at police, almost never qualify. Arrest for conduct (physical interference, true threats, refusing lawful orders to move back), not for words. An arrest for mouthing off is a retaliation claim waiting to happen (Nieves).

cases.name: Right to record police: Glik, Turner, Fields, and the Sixth Circuit
cases.cite: Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017); Fields v. Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir. 2017)
cases.facts: Glik: a Boston man filmed officers arresting someone on the Common and was arrested for wiretapping. Turner: a Texas man filming a police station from a public sidewalk was handcuffed and detained. Fields: Philadelphia officers detained and retaliated against bystanders filming police activity.
cases.held: The First, Third, Fifth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits have held that the public has a First Amendment right to record police performing their duties in public, subject to reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions. The Sixth Circuit (which covers Ohio) has not squarely decided it and has said the right was not clearly established for qualified-immunity purposes.
cases.forUs: Assume filming you is protected. Ohio is a one-party-consent state, so recording you in public isn't wiretapping, and the department's BWC directive assumes you're being recorded anyway. You can tell someone to step back to a reasonable distance for safety or to stop physically interfering; you cannot order them to stop recording, seize the phone, or delete footage. Seizing a phone requires a warrant or exigency and a reasonable belief it holds evidence of a crime. The Sixth Circuit's immunity position protects you civilly; it won't protect you from policy violations or from the video going viral.

cases.name: Obstruction and 'failure to comply' in Ohio
cases.cite: State v. Wellman, 2007-Ohio-2953 (2d Dist.); State v. Lazzaro, 76 Ohio St.3d 261 (1996); State v. Dowell, 2026-Ohio-4094
cases.facts: A line of Ohio cases defining obstructing official business (R.C. 2921.31). Lazzaro: giving a false statement to police can be obstruction when it actually hampers the investigation. Wellman and others: merely refusing to answer questions, arguing, or filming is not an 'act' that obstructs. Dowell: physically resisting a mental-health transport can be.
cases.held: Obstruction requires an affirmative act (not a mere refusal to cooperate or speak) that actually hampers or impedes an officer's lawful duty, done with purpose to obstruct. Lying can count; silence and criticism don't. Dowell confirms the act doesn't have to be independently illegal.
cases.forUs: 'He wouldn't answer my questions' is not obstruction. 'He gave a false name' can be. 'He stepped between me and the suspect' is. Write the specific act and specifically how it hampered you (delayed the arrest by X, forced you to call another unit, let the suspect flee). Resisting arrest (R.C. 2921.33) separately requires that the underlying arrest was lawful.

cases.name: Protests and crowd control: time, place, manner
cases.cite: Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989); Zorn v. Linton, 608 U.S. ___ (2026)
cases.facts: Ward: New York City required performers in Central Park to use city sound equipment and technicians to limit volume. Zorn: a sergeant used a wristlock on a protester after a warning.
cases.held: Government may impose content-neutral restrictions on the time, place, and manner of expression in public forums if they are narrowly tailored to a significant interest and leave ample alternative channels (Ward). Low-level force after a warning on a non-compliant protester did not violate clearly established law (Zorn).
cases.forUs: Dispersal orders and movement restrictions must be content-neutral and based on actual safety or traffic needs, not on what the crowd is saying. Give clear, audible orders, time to comply, and a route out, on camera. Arrests should be for identified conduct by identified individuals. 401.7 (labor disputes) and 409.2 (special events) have the department's procedures.

cases.name: Monell v. Department of Social Services / City of Canton v. Harris
cases.facts: Monell: NYC forced pregnant employees to take unpaid leave under official policy. Canton: a woman arrested in Canton, Ohio, slumped to the floor repeatedly at the station and got no medical attention; the city had given shift commanders no training on when to call for medical help.
cases.held: Cities are liable under § 1983 only for their own policies or customs, not simply because they employ the officer (Monell). Failure to train can be a 'policy' when the need for training is so obvious, and the inadequacy so likely to result in constitutional violations, that the city was deliberately indifferent (Canton).
cases.forUs: This is why the manual exists and why training records are kept. The city's defense in a lawsuit is 'we had a policy and trained him.' If you go outside the policy, you're on your own; if you follow it and it turns out to be bad policy, the city owns that. Canton (an Ohio case) is also the origin of 'if someone in custody looks like they need medical help, get it,' which 402.5 and 306.1 turn into rules.

cases.name: Qualified immunity: Harlow, Pearson, Hope, and Taylor
cases.cite: Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982); Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223 (2009); Hope v. Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730 (2002); Taylor v. Riojas, 592 U.S. 7 (2020)
cases.facts: The framework cases. Harlow created the modern objective test. Pearson let courts skip to the 'clearly established' question. Hope (a prisoner handcuffed to a hitching post for seven hours in the sun) and Taylor (an inmate kept in cells covered in feces and sewage for six days) held that some conduct is so obviously unconstitutional that no prior case with matching facts is needed.
cases.held: Officers are shielded from damages unless their conduct violated a constitutional right that was clearly established at the time, meaning existing precedent put the question beyond debate for a reasonable officer. Courts may decide the 'clearly established' prong first. Obvious violations don't require a case on point.
cases.forUs: Qualified immunity is a defense to personal money damages in federal civil suits. It does not stop criminal prosecution, discipline, decertification, the city settling, or your name in the paper. The Sixth Circuit has a deep body of excessive-force and search cases, so 'no case on point' is harder to claim here than in some circuits. The best immunity is following policy and law.

cases.name: Garrity v. New Jersey / Gardner v. Broderick
cases.facts: Garrity: New Jersey officers investigated for ticket-fixing were told they could refuse to answer but would be fired if they did; their answers were used to convict them. Gardner: an NYPD officer was fired for refusing to waive immunity before a grand jury.
cases.held: Statements compelled under threat of job loss cannot be used against the officer in a criminal prosecution (Garrity). An officer cannot be fired for refusing to waive the privilege against self-incrimination, but can be required to answer questions specifically, directly, and narrowly related to his duties if given immunity from criminal use (Gardner).
cases.forUs: In an administrative interview under 103.6, when you're ordered to answer, your answers are protected from criminal use, but you must answer truthfully and you can still be disciplined based on them. Lying in a Garrity interview is both a fireable offense and a Brady/Giglio problem. A criminal investigator can't use Garrity statements, which is why the two investigations are kept separate. Know your FOP contract rights on notice and representation.

cases.name: Ohio political-subdivision immunity: R.C. Chapter 2744 and Argabrite
cases.facts: A Montgomery County deputy pursued a burglary suspect who crashed head-on into Pamela Argabrite's car, badly injuring her. She sued the officers under state law.
cases.held: Under R.C. 2744.03(A)(6), individual officers are immune from state-law tort liability unless they acted with malicious purpose, in bad faith, or in a wanton or reckless manner. The Ohio Supreme Court rejected a 'no-proximate-cause' rule for pursuits and held the wanton-or-reckless standard applies; on these facts the officers were not reckless.
cases.forUs: In state court, the question for you personally is whether your conduct was 'wanton or reckless,' a high bar but one that a flagrant pursuit-policy violation can meet. The city separately faces liability for negligent emergency-vehicle operation in some circumstances (R.C. 2744.02(B)(1)). Pursuit policy (401.1) and emergency driving (303.1) exist as much to keep you inside 2744 immunity as to satisfy the Constitution.

cases.name: Medical needs in custody: Estelle, Farmer, and the Sixth Circuit's Brawner standard
cases.cite: Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976); Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825 (1994); Brawner v. Scott County, 14 F.4th 585 (6th Cir. 2021)
cases.facts: Estelle and Farmer established the deliberate-indifference standard for convicted prisoners. Brawner: a pretrial detainee in Tennessee had seizures after the jail stopped her prescribed medication; the Sixth Circuit addressed the standard for detainees after Kingsley.
cases.held: Deliberate indifference to serious medical needs violates the Constitution. For pretrial detainees in the Sixth Circuit, the test is modified-objective: the officer acted deliberately (not accidentally) and recklessly in the face of an unjustifiably high risk of harm that was either known or so obvious it should have been known.
cases.forUs: Someone in your custody who is injured, overdosing, having a seizure, saying they can't breathe, or who swallowed something gets medical care now, not after booking. Naloxone (401.28), trauma kits (401.30), and the detainee directives (402.5, 306.1) are the department's answer to this line of cases. 'I thought he was faking' is the sentence that loses.
